name: Illusion of asymmetric insight
statement: People believe they know their friends, their roommates and rival groups better than those others know them, because they take their own nature to be the harder one to read.
meaning: Pronin, Kruger, Savitsky and Ross put three claims on the table. The first is interpersonal: I know you better than you know me. The second is intrapersonal: I know myself better than you know yourself. The third follows from the other two, and says the gap between what a person knows about himself and what others know about him is wider for the self than for anyone else. The mechanism they propose is a rule about what counts as evidence. Overt behaviour is treated as diagnostic when somebody else produces it and as noise when one produces it oneself, while private thoughts and feelings are treated as diagnostic of the self alone. On that account the claim is not that one perceives more sharply. It is that one is harder to perceive.

origin.who: Emily Pronin, Justin Kruger, Kenneth Savitsky and Lee Ross
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper that names the effect and reports six studies, five on person perception and one on groups. Its samples run from 17 dyads to 200 students, and it reports t and F statistics without standardised effect sizes.

evidence: The six studies ran on undergraduates at Williams College, the University of Illinois and Stanford. In Study 1, 125 students rated a close friend on 11-point scales. They said they knew the friend, M = 8.89, better than the friend knew them, M = 8.64, t(124) = 2.26, p < .03, and 48 claimed the advantage against 24 who claimed the reverse, Z = 2.83, p < .005. Asked to circle one of ten partly submerged icebergs, they placed themselves deeper, 7.67 against 8.02 for the friend, t(124) = 3.19, p < .003. Study 2 gave 45 same-sex roommate pairs a 12-item composite on 9-point scales. Participants rated their knowledge of the roommate at 5.74 and the roommate's knowledge of them at 5.50, t(44) = 2.96, p < .005, and their own self-knowledge at 7.39 against the roommate's 6.70, t(44) = 5.54, p < .0001. The gap between their own self-knowledge and their roommate's knowledge of them, 1.89, exceeded the mirror-image gap of 0.97, t(44) = 5.51, p < .0001. That asymmetry was wider for private domains, 0.33, than public ones, 0.06, t(44) = 2.26, p < .05, and wider among pairs who were not close friends, 2.16 against 1.53, F(1, 42) = 5.04, p < .05. In Study 3, 200 students completed the sentence 'I am most like myself when I ...' for themselves and once for a friend. Two blind raters coded 72% of the completely private answers as being about the self and 66% of the answers naming contexts visible to intimates as being about the friend, chi-square(1, N = 200) = 17.45, p < .001. Study 4 brought together 17 previously unacquainted same-sex dyads. After a minute of conversation the asymmetry was marginal, 3.04 against 2.90, t(16) = 2.01, p < .10. After a 20-question exchange it reached 5.30 against 5.05, t(16) = 3.35, p < .005, and participants wrote 14.6 lines on what they had learned against 11.0 lines on what their partner had learned, t(16) = 4.93, p < .0001. In Study 5, 34 students rated word-fragment completions as more revealing of a peer than of themselves, t(30) = 2.29, p < .03 on the 21-item composite. Explaining their inferences, they quoted 3.94 of the partner's completions on average and 1.23 of their own, t(30) = 4.02, p < .0001. Study 6 asked 80 students about liberals and conservatives, pro-choice and pro-life advocates, and women and men. Each pairing produced a difference between the two groups' answers in the predicted direction, F(1, 65) = 6.22, F(1, 74) = 7.09 and F(1, 77) = 4.04.

replication.headline: The asymmetry turned up again in Korean and American samples, and no failure and no preregistered attempt was located.
replication.detail: Park, Choi and Cho ran three studies on Korean participants. Their abstract reports that the asymmetry was present in Study 1, that Study 2 found it to be a bias rather than an accurate report, and that Study 3 traced part of it to how people judge the situational variability of their own behaviour against other people's. Cho, Otani, Han and Van Horn then compared 306 American students, 114 men and 192 women, with 197 Korean students, 99 men and 98 women. Their abstract reports asymmetry on all three of their items, Know, Understand and Visibility, in horizontal relationships with best friends and in vertical relationships with parents, and greater asymmetry in the Korean group than the American group on Understand and Visibility. Both articles are paywalled and neither has a repository copy. Everything above was read from their abstracts at PubMed and Crossref, so this entry carries no replication effect size, no test statistic and no interval. Neither replication was preregistered. The search for a preregistered attempt or a reported failure ran across Crossref, PubMed, Semantic Scholar's citation list for the 2001 paper, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, OSF, PsyArXiv and the open web, and found neither.

study.cite: Cho, Y., Otani, H., Han, K., & Van Horn, K. R. (2010). Cultural differences in asymmetric beliefs of interpersonal knowledge in vertical and horizontal relationships. The Journal of General Psychology, 137(4), 343-361.

limits: The original evidence is thin study by study and consistent across studies. Its six samples were 125 students, 45 roommate pairs, 200 students, 17 dyads, 34 students and 80 students, drawn from three American colleges. None was preregistered. Every study asks one person about both self and other, which tells participants what is being compared. Study 6 does this in the open: a footnote records that all items for a given pair of groups appeared together, which the authors say made the comparison, and possibly the object of the investigation, explicit. Study 5 held in only one order. Participants who rated a peer's word completions before producing their own saw the peer's as more revealing, 3.54 against 2.93, t(18) = 2.95, p < .009, while those who rated their own first saw no difference, 2.86 against 2.92, t < 1, interaction F(1, 30) = 5.19, p < .03. The authors read that as doing the task teaching people to doubt word completions in general. The measures are beliefs about knowledge rather than knowledge. In Study 2 the roommate design sets two people's claims against each other, which shows the pair cannot both be right without showing which one is wrong, and Park and colleagues' abstract is the only located source that claims to have tested the beliefs against accuracy.
misreadings: The intergroup finding is usually retold as each side believing it understands the other better. The group means do not carry that. Liberals put their knowledge of conservatives at 5.81 against 5.14 the other way, t(34) = 3.10, p < .005, while conservatives gave 5.13 against 5.01, t(31) < 1. Pro-choice participants gave 5.42 against 4.47, t(53) = 4.09, p < .0001, and pro-life participants 5.30 against 5.01, t(21) < 1. Women and men both said women know men better, women putting the gap at 0.96, t(38) = 4.04, p < .0005, and men at 0.38, t(39) = 2.18, p < .05. What reached significance in each pairing is the difference between the two groups' answers, not a matching illusion held by each of them. The second misreading is one of scale. In Study 1 the two means sit a quarter of a point apart on an 11-point scale, and the authors write that the mean differences were small in absolute terms. Study 4's longer session gives 5.30 against 5.05 on a 9-point scale, and a footnote attributes the p value to a small within-subject error term rather than to a large difference. The third is that this is ordinary self-flattery, or the bias blind spot under a new name. Pronin and colleagues tested the first directly. Their roommates rated themselves as more competitive than their partners, 6.72 against 5.60, t(44) = 4.98, p < .0001, and as looking in the mirror more often, 6.16 against 5.03, t(44) = 4.78, p < .0001, neither of which flatters anybody. The blind spot is a different measurement. It asks how susceptible one is to named biases, and it has preregistered direct replications with pooled estimates. This asks who knows whom, and no preregistered replication of it was located.

sources.text: Pronin, E., Kruger, J., Savitsky, K., & Ross, L. (2001). You don't know me, but I know you: The illusion of asymmetric insight. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 639-656. Read in full from the first author's posted copy; the source for every figure in the evidence, limits and misreadings sections. Crossref records the third author's surname as 'Savtisky', and Princeton's record of the paper reverses the second and third authors and gives the last page as 655; the printed article's own header gives 639-656.

Park, J., Choi, I., & Cho, G. (2006). The actor-observer bias in beliefs of interpersonal insights. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 37(6), 630-642. Paywalled; only the abstract at Crossref was obtained, and no figure from it appears on this page.

Cho, Y., Otani, H., Han, K., & Van Horn, K. R. (2010). Cultural differences in asymmetric beliefs of interpersonal knowledge in vertical and horizontal relationships. The Journal of General Psychology, 137(4), 343-361. Paywalled; only the abstract at PubMed was obtained, and the sample counts quoted here are the ones it prints.

Steglich-Petersen, A., & Skipper, M. (2019). Explaining the illusion of asymmetric insight. Review of Philosophy and Psychology, 10, 769-786. A philosophical reanalysis with no new data, which argues that existing explanations of the illusion either invert the explanatory direction or fit the experiments too loosely. Only the abstract and bibliographic line at the publisher were obtained.
